questions.stem: A 2-year-old child has a generalized seizure during a febrile viral illness. There is no evidence of central nervous system infection. Which age range is used to define a febrile convulsion?

options.label: B
options.text: across the age range after puberty

questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe febrile convulsions as seizures associated with fever in children aged 6 months to 6 years without CNS infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the age range specified in standard definition.
- B. Febrile convulsions are a childhood diagnosis and are not defined for any age after puberty.

- C. This is older than the age range used.
- D. This age group is too young for the definition given.
- E. Neonatal seizures require evaluation for other causes and are outside this definition.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the age limits and the requirement that CNS infection be absent.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a febrile convulsion from a seizure caused by meningitis?

options.label: A
options.text: A febrile convulsion occurs without fever

options.label: B
options.text: A febrile convulsion is defined by an abnormal EEG

options.label: C
options.text: A febrile convulsion is typically focal

options.label: D
options.text: A febrile convulsion occurs with fever but without CNS infection

options.label: E
options.text: A febrile convulsion requires a positive CSF culture

questions.correctAnswerText: A febrile convulsion occurs with fever but without CNS infection
questions.initialExplanation: A febrile convulsion is associated with fever in the relevant childhood age group when CNS infection is absent; meningitis is an important alternative cause of fever with seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Fever is central to the definition.
- B. An abnormal EEG is not required to define a febrile convulsion.

- C. Febrile convulsions may be generalized or complex; they are not always focal.
- D. This is the key distinction in standard definition.
- E. A positive CSF culture supports CNS infection, which excludes a simple febrile convulsion diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The decisive distinction is whether there is an infection involving the CNS.

questions.stem: Which type of infection is the commonest fever focus associated with febrile convulsions?
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that the fever focus is commonly outside the CNS, most often a viral upper respiratory tract infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Endocarditis is not the commonest fever focus associated with febrile convulsions.
- B. Brain abscess is a CNS infection and is not the usual fever focus.
- C. Encephalitis is a CNS infection rather than an uncomplicated extracranial fever focus.

- D. Tuberculous meningitis is a CNS infection and therefore excludes a simple febrile convulsion.
- E. Viral URTI is identified as the usual focus.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The fever source is usually outside the brain and meninges.

questions.stem: Which feature classifies a febrile seizure as complex rather than simple?

options.label: B
options.text: A single brief seizure during the illness

options.label: C
options.text: A single seizure during 24 hours with no postictal deficit

options.label: D
options.text: Generalized tonic–clonic seizure lasting less than 15 minutes

options.label: E
options.text: Normal neurological status after the event

questions.initialExplanation: Complex febrile seizures may be focal, prolonged (more than 15 minutes), recurrent within 24 hours, or associated with postictal neurological deficits.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Focal onset is a defining complex feature.
- B. A single brief seizure is not by itself a complex feature.

- C. A single brief generalized event without deficit is simple.
- D. This pattern is typical of a simple febrile seizure.
- E. No postictal deficit is more consistent with simple febrile seizure.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the features used to separate simple from complex febrile seizures.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a simple febrile seizure?

options.label: A
options.text: Generalized tonic–clonic seizure lasting less than 15 minutes, occurring once in 24 hours

options.label: B
options.text: Seizure with persistent postictal focal weakness

options.label: D
options.text: Several seizures during the same 24-hour period

questions.correctAnswerText: Generalized tonic–clonic seizure lasting less than 15 minutes, occurring once in 24 hours
questions.initialExplanation: A simple febrile seizure is generalized, lasts less than 15 minutes, occurs only once within 24 hours, and has no postictal neurological deficit.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the defining simple febrile seizure pattern.
- B. A postictal focal deficit indicates a complex seizure.
- C. Meningitis is CNS infection and is not classified as a simple febrile seizure.

- D. Recurrent seizures within 24 hours define a complex febrile seizure.
- E. Focal onset and prolonged duration are complex features.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Check seizure type, duration, recurrence within 24 hours, and neurological recovery.

questions.stem: Which investigation is not routinely indicated in a child with a simple febrile convulsion,?

options.label: A
options.text: Appropriate assessment for meningitis when suspected

options.label: B
options.text: Clinical assessment for the fever focus

questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that CT brain and EEG are not indicated routinely in simple febrile convulsions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Assessment for meningitis is required when the clinical picture raises concern.
- B. Clinical evaluation is needed to identify the cause of fever.
- C. Testing may be guided by the child's clinical condition and suspected cause.
- D. Routine CT and EEG are not indicated in a simple febrile convulsion.
- E. Neurological examination is part of the clinical assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Distinguish targeted evaluation from routine neuroimaging or EEG in a simple event.

questions.stem: Which statement about antipyretics in children with febrile convulsions is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: They are used for comfort and fever, but have not been shown to prevent febrile seizures

options.label: B
options.text: They reliably prevent subsequent febrile seizures

options.label: C
options.text: They replace evaluation of the fever source

options.label: D
options.text: They prevent the later development of epilepsy

options.label: E
options.text: They are indicated after a complex seizure

questions.correctAnswerText: They are used for comfort and fever, but have not been shown to prevent febrile seizures
questions.initialExplanation: Antipyretics may be used for fever and comfort, but Clinical guidance notes that they have not been shown to prevent febrile seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This reflects the statement.
- B. Antipyretics do not reliably prevent recurrence.
- C. The fever source still requires clinical assessment and treatment when indicated.
- D. They have not been shown to prevent epilepsy.

- E. Antipyretics may be used for fever symptoms regardless of seizure complexity.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Separate symptomatic fever control from prevention of seizure recurrence.

---

## Epilepsy and Seizure Classification

questions.stem: How is epilepsy defined?

options.label: C
options.text: Two or more recurrent unprovoked seizures

options.label: E
options.text: An abnormal EEG without clinical seizures

questions.correctAnswerText: Two or more recurrent unprovoked seizures
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe epilepsy as recurrent (two or more) unprovoked seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. A single provoked febrile seizure does not meet this definition.
- B. Seizures may occur during sleep, but sleep occurrence is not the definition.
- C. Two or more unprovoked seizures form the definition given.
- D. Syncope is not an epileptic seizure.
- E. An EEG abnormality alone does not establish clinical epilepsy.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Focus on recurrence and the absence of an acute provoking cause.

questions.stem: A seizure begins in a localized group of neurons in one cerebral hemisphere. How is it classified?
questions.initialExplanation: Focal seizures arise from a localized neuronal network in one cerebral hemisphere.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Absence seizures are generalized non-motor seizures.

- B. Generalized seizures involve both hemispheres from onset.
- C. Atonic describes a seizure with loss of muscle tone, not its hemispheric onset.
- D. Febrile classification depends on age, fever, and absence of CNS infection, not anatomical onset alone.
- E. A seizure arising in one hemisphere is focal.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Classify seizures by where the abnormal electrical activity begins.

questions.stem: A child experiences focal sensory symptoms but remains fully aware throughout the event. Which seizure type is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: A focal seizure with intact consciousness is described as a simple partial seizure (focal seizure with awareness preserved).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Preserved awareness during focal symptoms fits a focal aware seizure.
- B. Atonic seizures cause transient loss of muscle tone.

- C. Impaired consciousness defines the older term complex partial seizure.
- D. A generalized tonic–clonic seizure involves bilateral motor activity and loss of consciousness.
- E. Absence seizures are brief generalized episodes of impaired awareness.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The level of awareness during a focal event determines this classification.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent episodes beginning with an unpleasant smell, followed by impaired awareness and lip-smacking. Which origin is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Temporal lobe seizures may produce olfactory or other sensory phenomena and automatisms such as lip-smacking, with impaired awareness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Temporal lobe onset is associated with smell or taste phenomena and automatisms.
- B. Primary motor cortex onset is more likely to produce focal motor signs.
- C. The spinal cord does not generate cortical focal seizures with impaired awareness.

- D. Occipital seizures more often produce visual phenomena.
- E. The cerebellum coordinates movement and is not the usual origin of epileptic automatisms.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Match the sensory aura and automatisms to the cerebral lobe described.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of a typical absence seizure?

options.label: A
options.text: Persistent unilateral weakness after the attack

options.label: D
options.text: Sudden brief impairment of consciousness with abrupt onset and termination

options.label: E
options.text: A preceding olfactory aura lasting several minutes

questions.correctAnswerText: Sudden brief impairment of consciousness with abrupt onset and termination
questions.initialExplanation: Typical absence seizures are brief, begin and end abruptly, and cause transient impairment of consciousness without a postictal phase.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Persistent focal weakness is not a typical absence feature.
- B. A prolonged postictal period is not typical of absence seizures.
- C. A focal motor march suggests focal seizure activity.
- D. This describes the typical absence pattern.
- E. An olfactory aura suggests focal temporal seizure activity.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Look for the short duration and immediate return to baseline.

questions.stem: Which EEG finding is classically associated with typical childhood absence seizures?
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include typical absence seizures as having bilaterally synchronous generalized spike-and-wave discharges at approximately 3–4 Hz.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave activity is the classic EEG pattern for typical absence seizures.
- B. Focal temporal slowing is not the typical absence EEG pattern.
- C. Centrotemporal spikes are associated with benign Rolandic epilepsy.
- D. Hypsarrhythmia is associated with infantile spasms.
- E. Burst suppression is a different EEG pattern seen in severe encephalopathy or under anaesthesia.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the characteristic frequency and generalized synchronous pattern.

questions.stem: Which medication is listed as the drug of choice for typical absence seizures?
questions.initialExplanation: Ethosuximide is listed as the drug of choice for typical absence seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Vigabatrin is used in infantile spasms.
- B. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.
- C. Ethosuximide is the listed first-choice drug for typical absence seizures.
- D. Baclofen is used for spasticity.

- E. Carbamazepine is associated with selected focal seizure types and may aggravate some generalized seizure types.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Match the generalized absence seizure syndrome to its listed first-line medication.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old infant develops clusters of brief flexor spasms, often around waking. Which epilepsy syndrome is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: West syndrome presents in infancy with brief repeated flexor or extensor spasms, often occurring in clusters around sleep–wake transitions.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Infantile spasms occur in infancy and produce repeated brief spasms.
- B. Typical absence epilepsy usually presents in school-age children with brief staring episodes.
- C. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy typically presents in adolescence, often shortly after waking.
- D. Lennox–Gastaut syndrome is characterized by multiple seizure types and developmental impairment, usually beginning in early childhood.

- E. Benign Rolandic epilepsy usually occurs in school-age children with focal seizures, often during sleep.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The age and clustered brief spasms distinguish this syndrome from school-age epilepsies.

questions.stem: Which EEG pattern is characteristic of infantile spasms (West syndrome)?
questions.initialExplanation: Hypsarrhythmia is the characteristic chaotic, high-voltage slow-wave EEG pattern described for infantile spasms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Centrotemporal spikes are associated with benign Rolandic epilepsy.
- B. Recognized features include a characteristic abnormal EEG pattern in infantile spasms.
- C. Focal occipital spikes are not the defining EEG pattern of West syndrome.

- D. Hypsarrhythmia is characteristic of West syndrome.
- E. This is associated with typical absence seizures.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Remember the distinctive chaotic, high-amplitude EEG background.

questions.stem: Which underlying condition is specifically associated with infantile spasms?
questions.initialExplanation: Tuberous sclerosis is listed as an important neurological cause of secondary infantile spasms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pyloric stenosis causes gastric outlet obstruction.
- B. Tuberous sclerosis is strongly associated with epilepsy and infantile spasms.
- C. Achondroplasia is a skeletal dysplasia and is not the association highlighted.
- D. Celiac disease is an enteropathy and is not the listed cause of West syndrome.
- E. Juvenile dermatomyositis is an inflammatory myopathy.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Connect infantile spasms with a neurocutaneous syndrome that causes seizures.

questions.stem: A school-aged child has nocturnal tonic–clonic seizures and focal facial or tongue symptoms with awareness preserved. EEG shows centrotemporal spikes. Which syndrome is most likely?

options.label: E
options.text: Benign focal epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (Rolandic epilepsy)

questions.correctAnswerText: Benign focal epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (Rolandic epilepsy)
questions.initialExplanation: Benign Rolandic epilepsy often presents in children aged approximately 4–10 years with nocturnal seizures or focal orofacial symptoms and centrotemporal spikes on EEG.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Lennox–Gastaut syndrome involves multiple seizure types and developmental impairment.
- B. West syndrome occurs in infancy with spasms and hypsarrhythmia.
- C. Typical absence epilepsy causes brief staring episodes with generalized spike-and-wave activity.

- D. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy typically presents around adolescence with myoclonic jerks after waking.
- E. This clinical pattern and EEG finding are characteristic of Rolandic epilepsy.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The age, nocturnal pattern, orofacial symptoms, and centrotemporal EEG focus form the key cluster.

questions.stem: Which statement about Lennox–Gastaut syndrome is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: It is associated with multiple seizure types and often poor response to anticonvulsant treatment

options.label: B
options.text: It usually resolves completely by adolescence without treatment

options.label: C
options.text: It usually presents with a single seizure type and normal development

options.label: E
options.text: It is defined by isolated absence seizures with 3-Hz spike-and-wave

questions.correctAnswerText: It is associated with multiple seizure types and often poor response to anticonvulsant treatment
questions.initialExplanation: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome is characterized by multiple seizure types, often an underlying brain injury or malformation, poor treatment response, and neurodevelopmental impairment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This summarizes the principal features.
- B. Clinical descriptions include poor response and neurodevelopmental impairment rather than predictable spontaneous remission.
- C. Multiple seizure types and developmental problems are typical, not a single seizure with normal development.
- D. Lennox–Gastaut syndrome begins in early childhood, not only adulthood.

- E. Isolated absence seizures with 3-Hz spike-and-wave suggest typical absence epilepsy.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Focus on seizure diversity, developmental course, and treatment resistance.

questions.stem: A teenager experiences myoclonic jerks, generalized tonic–clonic seizures, and sometimes absences, mostly shortly after waking. Which syndrome is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is described as causing myoclonic, generalized tonic–clonic, and sometimes absence seizures, commonly shortly after waking.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. West syndrome occurs in infancy with clustered spasms.
- B. Lennox–Gastaut syndrome typically begins in early childhood and involves developmental impairment and multiple seizure types.
- C. Rolandic epilepsy causes focal orofacial seizures in younger children.
- D. Febrile seizures occur in the setting of fever in the defined age range.

- E. This is the characteristic seizure pattern and timing described for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The adolescent age and seizures soon after waking are important clues.

---

## Status Epilepticus

questions.stem: According to the newer time-based definition quoted, when should a continuing convulsive seizure be treated as status epilepticus?
questions.initialExplanation: Although the older definition used 30 minutes, Clinical guidance notes the newer operational definition of 5 minutes or more for ongoing seizure activity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Thirty seconds is shorter than the operational threshold described.
- B. Thirty minutes reflects the older definition rather than the newer threshold.
- C. Status epilepticus is an acute time-critical event, not a multi-day criterion.

- D. Two minutes is below the newer threshold given.
- E. Five minutes or more is the newer operational definition emphasized in the notes.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Distinguish the historic 30-minute definition from the newer operational threshold.

questions.stem: A child continues convulsing despite an adequate first benzodiazepine and a second appropriate anticonvulsant. How is this classified?
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe refractory status epilepticus as clinical or electrographic seizures persisting after an adequate benzodiazepine and a second appropriate anticonvulsant.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the definition of refractory status epilepticus.
- B. Syncope is transient cerebral hypoperfusion and does not fit ongoing electrographic seizure.
- C. Absence epilepsy does not describe persistent convulsive activity despite rescue therapy.
- D. The child is still actively convulsing rather than in a postictal state.

- E. A prolonged ongoing seizure after sequential treatment is not a simple febrile seizure.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Count the failure of the initial benzodiazepine and the next appropriate anticonvulsant.

---

## Conditions Mimicking Seizures

questions.stem: A toddler becomes upset, cries, holds the breath in expiration, turns blue, and briefly loses consciousness before rapidly recovering. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Cyanotic breath-holding spells are commonly triggered by upset or crying, followed by expiratory breath-holding, cyanosis, and sometimes brief loss of consciousness.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the typical sequence of a cyanotic breath-holding spell.
- B. Absence seizures are not usually triggered by crying and do not cause this expiratory breath-holding sequence.
- C. Pallid spells are typically triggered by pain and a vagal bradycardic response with pallor.
- D. Infantile spasms occur in infancy as brief repeated muscle contractions.

- E. Meningitis usually causes systemic illness and neurological signs rather than stereotyped brief spells after upset.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The emotional trigger, expiratory breath-holding, and color change identify the spell type.

questions.stem: A toddler becomes pale and briefly loses consciousness immediately after a painful minor injury. Which mechanism best explains this pallid breath-holding spell?

options.label: B
options.text: Acute intracranial hemorrhage in each case

questions.initialExplanation: Pallid breath-holding spells are triggered by pain and involve a reflex vagal response with bradycardia and transient cerebral hypoperfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hyperglycemia is not the mechanism described.
- B. A minor painful trigger does not imply intracranial hemorrhage.
- C. An epileptic discharge is not the mechanism of a typical pallid breath-holding spell.
- D. This is the mechanism described.
- E. Bronchospasm does not explain the reflex bradycardic pallid spell.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The trigger is pain, and the child becomes pale rather than cyanotic.

questions.stem: A child faints after standing for a prolonged period in a hot, crowded environment. Brief clonic movements occur for a few seconds, followed by spontaneous recovery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Vasovagal syncope may occur with heat, prolonged standing, or fear; brief clonic movements can accompany fainting and do not by themselves prove epilepsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Focal epilepsy is not defined by a typical vasovagal trigger and spontaneous rapid recovery after fainting.
- B. Lennox–Gastaut syndrome is a childhood epilepsy syndrome with multiple seizure types.

- C. Infantile spasms are brief clusters in infants, not fainting after standing.
- D. This is the typical trigger pattern for vasovagal syncope described.
- E. Meningitis causes an infectious syndrome rather than an isolated vasovagal faint.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider the situational trigger and rapid spontaneous recovery.


---

## Meningitis

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant has fever, poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, and a tense bulging anterior fontanelle. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?
questions.initialExplanation: Meningitis in infants may present with nonspecific systemic symptoms, and a tense or bulging anterior fontanelle may indicate raised intracranial pressure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Functional abdominal pain does not explain fever and a tense fontanelle.
- B. Duchenne muscular dystrophy causes progressive muscle weakness, not acute febrile illness.
- C. Breath-holding spells are brief triggered events and do not cause persistent systemic illness.

- D. Migraine does not explain an infant's bulging fontanelle and systemic illness.
- E. These systemic and fontanelle findings are compatible with meningitis and require urgent assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Infants may lack the classic meningeal signs seen in older children.

questions.stem: A child is supine with hips and knees flexed to 90 degrees. Passive extension of the knee causes pain and resistance. Which meningeal sign is positive?
questions.initialExplanation: Kernig sign is positive when passive extension of the knee from a flexed hip-and-knee position causes pain or resistance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Babinski sign is an abnormal plantar response.
- B. Rovsing sign is right iliac fossa pain elicited by left-sided abdominal palpation.
- C. Brudzinski sign involves reflex flexion of the hips and knees during passive neck flexion.
- D. This describes Kernig sign.
- E. Macewen sign is a skull percussion sign associated with hydrocephalus.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The examiner keeps the hip flexed and extends the knee.

questions.stem: When the neck of a supine child is passively flexed, both hips and knees flex involuntarily. Which sign is this?
questions.initialExplanation: Brudzinski sign is reflex flexion of the hips and knees following passive neck flexion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the definition of Brudzinski sign.
- B. Gower sign is used to demonstrate proximal muscle weakness.

- C. Murphy sign is associated with gallbladder inflammation.
- D. Rovsing sign is an abdominal examination sign.
- E. Kernig sign is elicited by passive knee extension with the hip flexed.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The key movement is involuntary hip and knee flexion when the neck is flexed.

questions.stem: Which finding is an absolute contraindication to immediate lumbar puncture in a child with suspected meningitis?

options.label: B
options.text: A history of uncomplicated febrile seizure

questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include cardiorespiratory instability, signs of raised intracranial pressure, coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia, focal neurological signs, and local infection at the puncture site as contraindications to lumbar puncture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Shock or cardiorespiratory instability makes lumbar puncture unsafe until stabilization.
- B. An uncomplicated febrile seizure history alone is not listed as a contraindication.
- C. Fever alone is not listed as an absolute contraindication.
- D. Normal consciousness is not a contraindication.

- E. A mild sore throat is not an absolute contraindication.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Prioritize physiological instability and signs that raise the risk of herniation or bleeding.

questions.stem: A child with suspected bacterial meningitis has signs of raised intracranial pressure, so lumbar puncture is deferred. What should happen to antibiotic treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Start appropriate empirical antibiotics without delay

options.label: B
options.text: Wait for a CT scan before any treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Withhold antibiotics until CSF is obtained

questions.correctAnswerText: Start appropriate empirical antibiotics without delay
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is that when lumbar puncture is contraindicated, antibiotics must not be delayed while waiting for the procedure or further investigations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Empirical antibiotics should be started promptly when LP is unsafe or delayed.
- B. Imaging should not delay urgent antibiotics when clinical suspicion is high.
- C. Antipyretics alone do not treat bacterial meningitis.

- D. Delaying treatment risks progression of a life-threatening infection.
- E. Oral outpatient treatment is not adequate for suspected bacterial meningitis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The contraindication changes the timing of LP, not the urgency of antimicrobial treatment.

questions.stem: Which CSF profile is most consistent with bacterial meningitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Turbid CSF, neutrophil predominance, high protein, low glucose

options.label: B
options.text: Lymphocyte predominance with low protein and high glucose

options.label: C
options.text: Clear CSF, lymphocyte predominance, normal glucose, mildly increased protein

options.label: D
options.text: Clear CSF, normal cells, low protein, high glucose

options.label: E
options.text: Normal CSF cell count with normal protein and glucose

questions.correctAnswerText: Turbid CSF, neutrophil predominance, high protein, low glucose
questions.initialExplanation: Bacterial meningitis typically produces neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and reduced CSF glucose; the fluid may appear turbid.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the typical bacterial CSF pattern described.
- B. This combination does not match the typical bacterial CSF pattern.

- C. This pattern is more consistent with viral meningitis.
- D. This is not the typical bacterial inflammatory profile.
- E. Normal CSF findings would not support bacterial meningitis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Compare the predominant white-cell type, protein concentration, and CSF glucose.

questions.stem: Which CSF pattern is most consistent with viral meningitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Lymphocyte predominance, normal or mildly raised protein, and usually normal glucose

options.label: B
options.text: Neutrophil predominance, markedly high protein, and low glucose

options.label: C
options.text: No cells, very low protein, and absent glucose

options.label: D
options.text: Markedly low glucose with very high neutrophils in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Positive Gram stain with bacterial growth in culture

questions.correctAnswerText: Lymphocyte predominance, normal or mildly raised protein, and usually normal glucose
questions.initialExplanation: Viral meningitis usually causes lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal or mildly elevated protein, and normal glucose, although exceptions occur with some viruses.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the usual viral CSF profile listed.
- B. This is more typical of bacterial meningitis.
- C. The CSF is not expected to be acellular with absent glucose.
- D. This describes a bacterial rather than usual viral pattern.

- E. Positive Gram stain and bacterial growth support bacterial infection.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Viral CSF usually preserves glucose and is predominantly lymphocytic.

questions.stem: Which is the most common long-term neurological sequela of bacterial meningitis emphasized?
questions.initialExplanation: Sensorineural hearing loss is highlighted as the most common long-term sequela, related to inflammatory injury to cochlear hair cells.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Cleft palate is a congenital orofacial anomaly.
- B. Sensorineural hearing loss is the key long-term complication emphasized.
- C. Achalasia is an esophageal motility disorder.
- D. Nephrotic syndrome is a renal condition and is not the commonest long-term neurological sequela.

- E. Pyloric stenosis is an unrelated gastric outlet disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Think of injury to the cochlea and the importance of hearing follow-up after meningitis.

questions.stem: Household contacts of a child with meningococcal meningitis require which preventive measure?

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate lumbar puncture for close contacts

options.label: E
options.text: No action if they are asymptomatic

questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes chemoprophylaxis for household contacts to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage in meningococcal infection; vaccination is also important for prevention.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Anticonvulsants are not used as prophylaxis for meningococcal infection.
- B. Lumbar puncture is not performed routinely in asymptomatic contacts.

- C. Chemoprophylaxis is used to reduce carriage and secondary cases.
- D. Dietary gluten restriction is unrelated.
- E. Close contacts require assessment and prophylaxis even if asymptomatic.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- The objective is to eradicate carriage in close contacts and reduce secondary transmission.

## Meningococcal Infection

questions.stem: A previously healthy child presents with high fever, toxic appearance, rapidly spreading petechiae and purpura, delayed capillary refill, and hypotension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Meningococcal septicemia can progress rapidly with high fever, toxicity, petechial or purpuric rash, and septic shock.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. A febrile seizure does not explain purpura and shock.
- B. Migraine does not cause septic shock or purpuric rash.
- C. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness, not an acute purpuric septic illness.

- D. This is the classic rapidly progressive clinical picture described for meningococcemia.
- E. Cerebral palsy is a chronic non-progressive motor disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints: - A febrile child with a non-blanching purpuric rash and poor perfusion is a medical emergency.

questions.stem: A child is suspected of having meningococcal septicemia. Which immediate treatment principle is emphasized?

options.label: A
options.text: Resuscitation and immediate empirical intravenous third-generation cephalosporin

options.label: B
options.text: Delay antibiotics until lumbar puncture is completed

options.label: C
options.text: Oral antibiotics after waiting for culture results

questions.correctAnswerText: Resuscitation and immediate empirical intravenous third-generation cephalosporin
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is ABC resuscitation, immediate empirical IV ceftriaxone (or an appropriate third-generation cephalosporin), urgent critical care, and isolation/notification.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Immediate resuscitation and IV empirical antibiotics are essential.
- B. Antibiotics must not be delayed for lumbar puncture in a critically ill child.
- C. Waiting for cultures delays life-saving treatment.
- D. Corticosteroids alone do not treat the infection or septic shock.

- E. Outpatient management is unsafe in suspected meningococcal septicemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Recognize that treatment must begin before microbiological confirmation in this emergency.

## Encephalitis

questions.stem: Which finding best distinguishes encephalitis from isolated meningitis?

options.label: B
options.text: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma with altered behavior, seizures, or focal neurological signs

options.label: E
options.text: Inflammation limited to the meninges without cerebral symptoms

questions.correctAnswerText: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma with altered behavior, seizures, or focal neurological signs
questions.initialExplanation: Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma and can cause altered behavior or consciousness, seizures, raised intracranial pressure, and neurological deficits.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. A skin rash alone does not define encephalitis.
- B. This describes parenchymal brain involvement and its neurological manifestations.
- C. Chronic proximal weakness suggests a myopathy rather than encephalitis.
- D. A skull-shape abnormality is unrelated to acute brain inflammation.

- E. This describes meningitis without parenchymal encephalitis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Look for cerebral dysfunction in addition to systemic or meningeal symptoms.

questions.stem: A child has fever, behavioral change, seizures, and MRI abnormalities involving the temporal lobes. Which viral cause must be treated empirically while awaiting confirmation?
questions.initialExplanation: HSV encephalitis can cause severe temporal-lobe disease. Recommended management includes initial high-dose IV acyclovir in children with encephalitis until HSV has been excluded.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Rotavirus is primarily an enteric pathogen and is not the classic temporal-lobe encephalitis cause.
- B. HPV is not the usual cause of acute encephalitis.
- C. Norovirus causes acute gastroenteritis.
- D. HSV is an important treatable cause of temporal-lobe encephalitis.
- E. Rhinovirus is not the characteristic virus associated with this temporal-lobe pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Temporal-lobe involvement is a high-yield clue to an encephalitis that requires empiric antiviral treatment.

questions.stem: Which CSF pattern is commonly described in viral encephalitis?

options.label: B
options.text: Turbid fluid with neutrophilia and very low glucose in typical presentations

options.label: C
options.text: Positive bacterial Gram stain in each case

options.label: D
options.text: High red cells with no white cells as the defining finding

options.label: E
options.text: Clear fluid with lymphocytosis, normal or raised protein, and usually normal glucose

questions.correctAnswerText: Clear fluid with lymphocytosis, normal or raised protein, and usually normal glucose
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include viral encephalitis CSF as usually clear, with lymphocytosis, normal or mildly elevated protein, and normal glucose.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. An acellular CSF with absent protein is not the expected profile.
- B. This is more suggestive of bacterial meningitis.
- C. A positive bacterial Gram stain is not expected in viral encephalitis.
- D. Red cells may be seen in some HSV cases, but this is not the defining general CSF pattern described.

- E. This is the typical viral CSF profile given.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Use the usual viral inflammatory pattern while remembering that CSF can vary by cause and timing.

## Neural Tube Defects

questions.stem: Neural tube defects arise from failure of normal neural tube closure during which period of development?

options.label: E
options.text: After the first year of life

questions.initialExplanation: The neural tube normally forms and closes during the first 28 days following conception; failure of closure produces neural tube defects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. The defect arises during early embryogenesis, not at delivery.
- B. This is the critical developmental period stated.
- C. Puberty is unrelated to neural tube formation.

- D. Neural tube closure has already occurred long before the third trimester.
- E. The neural tube forms prenatally during early embryogenesis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the very early embryological timing of neural tube closure.

questions.stem: Which maternal factor is a major modifiable risk factor for neural tube defects?
questions.initialExplanation: Folic acid deficiency is a major risk factor for neural tube defects; standard guidance also lists maternal diabetes and anticonvulsant exposure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Iron supplementation is not the risk factor identified.
- B. Adequate folate intake is protective rather than a risk factor.
- C. Influenza vaccination is not a recognized cause of neural tube defects.
- D. Folate deficiency increases the risk of neural tube defects.
- E. Calcium intake is not the principal risk factor listed.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Identify the vitamin whose supplementation is used specifically to prevent neural tube defects.

questions.stem: A child has a small vertebral arch defect with no protrusion of meninges or spinal cord. The finding is incidental, and there is no neurological deficit at birth. What is the diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Spina bifida occulta is a defect in the vertebral arch without protrusion of meninges or spinal cord and is often asymptomatic.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Encephalocele is herniation of intracranial contents through a skull defect.
- B. Anencephaly involves failure of development of much of the cranium and brain.

- C. This is the definition of spina bifida occulta.
- D. Myelomeningocele contains meninges and spinal cord tissue.
- E. Meningocele involves protrusion of meninges through a vertebral defect.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Differentiate a hidden vertebral arch defect from lesions with a protruding sac.

questions.stem: Which structure protrudes through the vertebral defect in a meningocele?

options.label: B
options.text: Spinal cord and meninges together in each case

options.label: D
options.text: Meninges, with the spinal cord remaining normal

questions.correctAnswerText: Meninges, with the spinal cord remaining normal
questions.initialExplanation: In meningocele, the meninges protrude through the vertebral arch defect while the spinal cord is usually normal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Cerebral cortex does not protrude through a spinal vertebral defect.
- B. Protrusion of both meninges and spinal cord describes myelomeningocele.
- C. An intervertebral disc is not the content of a meningocele.

- D. This describes meningocele.
- E. Cerebellar and brainstem herniation is associated with Chiari malformation.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The key distinction from myelomeningocele is whether neural tissue is included in the sac.

questions.stem: A newborn with myelomeningocele has lower-limb paralysis, sensory loss, and bladder dysfunction. Which associated brain abnormality is a major cause of hydrocephalus in these patients?
questions.initialExplanation: Myelomeningocele is commonly associated with Arnold–Chiari type II malformation, which can disrupt CSF flow and lead to hydrocephalus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pituitary adenoma does not explain the myelomeningocele association.
- B. Rolandic epilepsy is unrelated to the spinal dysraphism and hydrocephalus association.

- C. Cortical dysplasia is not the specific cause described.
- D. This is the association highlighted.
- E. Dandy–Walker malformation is another cause of obstructive hydrocephalus but is not the key association here.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Connect lumbosacral myelomeningocele with downward displacement at the foramen magnum.

## Hydrocephalus

questions.stem: Hydrocephalus is defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced production of CSF with small ventricles

options.label: B
options.text: Atrophy of the cerebral cortex without ventricular change

options.label: C
options.text: Enlargement of cerebral ventricles due to excessive accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid

options.label: D
options.text: Increased skull thickness from bone overgrowth

questions.correctAnswerText: Enlargement of cerebral ventricles due to excessive accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid
questions.initialExplanation: Hydrocephalus is enlargement of the cerebral ventricles resulting from excessive accumulation of CSF.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Reduced CSF production would not produce the described ventricular enlargement.

- B. Cortical atrophy alone is not the definition of hydrocephalus.
- C. This is the definition given.
- D. Skull bone overgrowth is not hydrocephalus.
- E. Peripheral neuritis affects peripheral nerves rather than CSF spaces.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Focus on ventricular enlargement caused by excess CSF accumulation.

questions.stem: Which mechanism can cause hydrocephalus?

options.label: B
options.text: Increased CSF production, impaired absorption, or obstruction to CSF flow

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased CSF production, impaired absorption, or obstruction to CSF flow
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include three mechanisms: increased production, defective absorption, and obstruction within the ventricular system.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Reduced production does not explain excess CSF accumulation.
- B. These are the three mechanisms identified.
- C. Peripheral nerve conduction is unrelated to CSF dynamics.
- D. Muscle tone does not cause ventricular dilatation.
- E. Red-cell production is unrelated to hydrocephalus.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the three ways the balance between CSF production, flow, and absorption can be disrupted.

questions.stem: A child has hydrocephalus caused by aqueduct of Sylvius stenosis. How is this classified?

options.label: C
options.text: Communicating hydrocephalus due to impaired absorption

questions.initialExplanation: Aqueductal stenosis obstructs CSF flow within the ventricular system and causes non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is not the congenital aqueductal stenosis pattern described.

- B. CSF overproduction is a separate, uncommon mechanism such as choroid plexus papilloma.
- C. Communicating hydrocephalus results from impaired absorption after CSF leaves the ventricles.
- D. This is the classification of hydrocephalus due to aqueductal obstruction.
- E. Ex-vacuo enlargement reflects tissue loss rather than obstruction.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Determine whether the problem blocks CSF flow within the ventricular system.

questions.stem: Which clinical sign is particularly characteristic of hydrocephalus in an infant?
questions.initialExplanation: Sunsetting of the eyes (fixed downward gaze) is an advanced sign of hydrocephalus in infants, often associated with increased intracranial pressure.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Gottron papules are seen in juvenile dermatomyositis.
- B. Gower sign indicates proximal muscle weakness, classically in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- C. Rovsing sign is an abdominal sign of appendicitis.
- D. Sunsetting gaze is a characteristic advanced infant sign described.
- E. Calf pseudohypertrophy is associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Look for the abnormal downward eye position in an infant with an enlarging head.

questions.stem: Which investigation is commonly used as the initial imaging study to assess ventricular dilatation in a neonate or infant with an open fontanelle?
questions.initialExplanation: Cranial ultrasound can assess ventricular size in neonates and infants through the open fontanelle.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. EEG evaluates cerebral electrical activity rather than ventricular size.
- B. Cranial ultrasound is the initial imaging modality listed for assessing ventricular dilatation in infants.
- C. Barium swallow evaluates the esophagus and upper gastrointestinal tract.

- D. An abdominal radiograph does not assess cerebral ventricles.
- E. Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerves.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Use the open fontanelle as an acoustic window to examine the ventricles.

questions.stem: Which is a recognized complication of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt?
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include infection (commonly Staphylococcus epidermidis) and mechanical blockage as important VP shunt complications; shunt nephritis is uncommon.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pyloric hypertrophy causes gastric outlet obstruction.
- B. Myasthenic crisis is respiratory weakness from neuromuscular transmission failure.

- C. Both infection and blockage are recognized VP shunt complications.
- D. Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy.
- E. Cleft palate is a congenital orofacial malformation.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Remember both infectious and mechanical causes of shunt malfunction.

## Upper and Lower Motor Neuron Lesions

topics.name: Upper and Lower Motor Neuron Lesions

questions.stem: Which examination pattern is most consistent with an upper motor neuron lesion?

options.label: B
options.text: Flaccid weakness with marked muscle fasciculations

options.label: C
options.text: Spasticity, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response

options.label: D
options.text: Normal tone with fatigability and normal reflexes

questions.correctAnswerText: Spasticity, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response
questions.initialExplanation: Upper motor neuron lesions classically cause increased tone, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This pattern suggests a lower motor neuron lesion.
- B. Fasciculations and reduced reflexes support lower motor neuron involvement.
- C. This is the classic upper motor neuron pattern described.
- D. Fatigability with preserved reflexes is characteristic of myasthenia gravis.
- E. This pattern is associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Compare tone, deep tendon reflexes, and the plantar response.

questions.stem: Which finding favors a lower motor neuron lesion over an upper motor neuron lesion?

options.label: B
options.text: Fasciculations with hypotonia and reduced reflexes

questions.correctAnswerText: Fasciculations with hypotonia and reduced reflexes
questions.initialExplanation: Lower motor neuron lesions produce hypotonia, reduced or absent reflexes, weakness, and may cause fasciculations and muscle wasting.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hyperreflexia is an upper motor neuron sign.
- B. This combination is characteristic of lower motor neuron involvement.
- C. An extensor plantar response is an upper motor neuron sign.
- D. Spasticity is associated with upper motor neuron lesions.
- E. Clonus is associated with upper motor neuron dysfunction.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Look for denervation signs and reduced reflex activity.

questions.stem: A child can move a limb through its full range of motion only when gravity is eliminated. What is the muscle power grade?
questions.initialExplanation: Grade 2 power means active movement is possible when gravity is eliminated, but not against gravity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Grade 1 means visible contraction without limb movement.
- B. Grade 2 means active movement with gravity eliminated.
- C. Grade 3 means active movement against gravity.
- D. Grade 4 means movement against gravity and partial resistance.

- E. Grade 0 means no visible contraction.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Recall the difference between movement with gravity eliminated and movement against gravity.

## Cerebral Palsy

questions.stem: Cerebral palsy is best defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: An acute infection of the meninges

options.label: B
options.text: A progressive degenerative disorder of the spinal cord

options.label: C
options.text: A disorder of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive insult to the developing brain

options.label: D
options.text: A transient seizure disorder triggered by fever

options.label: E
options.text: A primary muscle disease that begins in adolescence

questions.correctAnswerText: A disorder of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive insult to the developing brain
questions.initialExplanation: Cerebral palsy is a disorder of movement and posture resulting from a non-progressive injury or insult to the developing brain.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Meningitis is an acute infection and is one possible acquired cause of brain injury, not the definition of CP.

- B. CP is non-progressive, unlike degenerative spinal cord disorders.
- C. This is the definition.
- D. Febrile seizures are episodic seizures associated with fever and do not define CP.
- E. Primary muscle diseases cause progressive weakness rather than the defining CP brain injury.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The key distinction is a static brain insult with persistent motor consequences.

questions.stem: Which type of cerebral palsy is the commonest and accounts for approximately 80–90% of cases?
questions.initialExplanation: Spastic cerebral palsy is the commonest type, accounting for approximately 80–90% of cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Spastic CP is the commonest form and is associated with pyramidal tract injury.
- B. Dyskinetic CP is associated with extrapyramidal dysfunction and involuntary movements.
- C. Atonic CP is not the commonest type listed.
- D. Ataxic CP is associated with cerebellar dysfunction and is less common.
- E. Mixed CP combines features of more than one motor phenotype.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the commonest motor phenotype and its approximate proportion.

questions.stem: A child with cerebral palsy has increased tone, brisk reflexes, and an extensor plantar response. Which neuroanatomical pathway is most likely affected?
questions.initialExplanation: Spastic cerebral palsy results from injury to the pyramidal or corticospinal tract and produces upper motor neuron signs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. A peripheral sensory nerve lesion does not produce this UMN pattern.
- B. Autonomic ganglia do not explain the motor examination pattern.

- C. Neuromuscular junction disorders cause fatigable weakness rather than spasticity and hyperreflexia.
- D. The corticospinal tract is associated with spastic CP and UMN signs.
- E. Primary muscle disease causes myopathic weakness, not an extensor plantar response.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Link spasticity and hyperreflexia to the descending motor pathway.

questions.stem: A child with cerebral palsy has involuntary writhing movements, dystonia, and variable abnormal tone. Which type is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Dyskinetic cerebral palsy is associated with extrapyramidal or basal ganglia injury and may produce chorea, athetosis, and dystonia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Dyskinetic CP causes involuntary movements such as chorea, athetosis, and dystonia.
- B. Spastic CP produces increased tone and pyramidal signs.
- C. Ataxic CP causes incoordination, intention tremor, and gait ataxia.
- D. Atonic CP is characterized by reduced tone rather than the described dyskinesia.
- E. Monoplegic CP describes distribution to one limb and does not define the involuntary movement pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Distinguish involuntary movement disorders from spasticity and cerebellar incoordination.

questions.stem: Which clinical feature is most characteristic of ataxic cerebral palsy?

options.label: B
options.text: Proximal muscle weakness with Gower sign

options.label: C
options.text: Incoordination, intention tremor, and ataxic gait

questions.correctAnswerText: Incoordination, intention tremor, and ataxic gait
questions.initialExplanation: Ataxic CP results from cerebellar involvement and causes poor balance, incoordination, intention tremor, and an ataxic gait.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Ptosis and diplopia with fatigability suggest myasthenia gravis.
- B. Gower sign and proximal weakness suggest Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

- C. This is the characteristic cerebellar pattern in ataxic CP.
- D. Spasticity and scissoring are features of spastic CP.
- E. Ascending flaccid paralysis suggests Guillain–Barré syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Cerebellar dysfunction affects coordination, balance, and the accuracy of movement.

questions.stem: Which early developmental finding is a warning sign for cerebral palsy?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal symmetric hand use at 18 months

options.label: C
options.text: Independent walking at the expected age

options.label: D
options.text: Early hand preference before 12 months of age

questions.correctAnswerText: Early hand preference before 12 months of age
questions.initialExplanation: Early hand preference before 12 months may indicate asymmetric motor function and is a red flag for cerebral palsy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Symmetric use is reassuring rather than a warning sign.
- B. Persistence rather than normal resolution of primitive reflexes is concerning.
- C. Expected motor milestone attainment is not itself a red flag.
- D. Early hand preference before one year may reflect an abnormal unilateral motor deficit.
- E. Normal feeding and motor development are reassuring findings.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Marked early handedness may reflect an underlying unilateral motor impairment.

questions.stem: Which investigation is required to diagnose cerebral palsy in most children?

options.label: A
options.text: Lumbar puncture in children in routine care

options.label: B
options.text: Muscle biopsy in children in routine care

options.label: C
options.text: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, with investigations guided by the need to identify cause or exclude alternatives

options.label: D
options.text: Nerve conduction study as the definitive test

options.label: E
options.text: EEG in children in routine care regardless of seizure history

questions.correctAnswerText: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, with investigations guided by the need to identify cause or exclude alternatives
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that CP is diagnosed mainly clinically; neuroimaging, metabolic or infection screening, and EEG are selected according to the suspected cause or associated features.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Lumbar puncture is not routinely required to diagnose CP.
- B. Muscle biopsy is not a routine diagnostic test for CP.
- C. This reflects the diagnostic approach described.
- D. Nerve conduction studies are not the definitive diagnostic test for CP.

- E. EEG is indicated when seizures are suspected, not universally.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The diagnosis is clinical; investigations help explain etiology or exclude progressive mimics.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes cerebral palsy from a neurodegenerative disorder?

options.label: A
options.text: CP is non-progressive, whereas neurodegenerative disorders show progressive deterioration

options.label: B
options.text: CP is usually progressive while neurodegenerative disease is static

options.label: C
options.text: Both conditions are typically associated with hepatosplenomegaly

options.label: D
options.text: Neurodegenerative disease has no family history

options.label: E
options.text: CP typically causes progressive head enlargement

questions.correctAnswerText: CP is non-progressive, whereas neurodegenerative disorders show progressive deterioration
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance contrasts the non-progressive course of CP with the progressive course of neurodegenerative disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the key distinction in the comparison table.
- B. This reverses the expected courses.
- C. Hepatosplenomegaly may suggest some metabolic or storage disorders but is not universal in either condition.
- D. A family history may be present in neurodegenerative diseases, but it is not universal.

- E. CP does not invariably cause progressive head enlargement.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Follow the child's developmental trajectory over time: static versus progressive.

## Spinal Muscular Atrophy

questions.stem: Spinal muscular atrophy primarily affects which anatomical structure?

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and motor cranial nerve nuclei

questions.correctAnswerText: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord and motor cranial nerve nuclei
questions.initialExplanation: SMA is a degenerative disorder of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord and motor nuclei in the brainstem.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. SMA is primarily a motor neuron disorder, not a sensory ganglion disorder.

- B. This is the site of neuronal loss described in SMA.
- C. Meningeal inflammation is unrelated to SMA.
- D. Cerebellar degeneration is not the primary pathology of SMA.
- E. The primary lesion is in motor neurons rather than exclusively at the neuromuscular junction.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Identify the motor neuron population that degenerates in spinal muscular atrophy.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant has severe symmetrical hypotonia and weakness. Which SMA type is most consistent with onset before 6 months?
questions.initialExplanation: SMA type 1 is the severe acute infantile form, with onset from birth to 6 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Type 2 generally presents later, between 6 and 18 months.
- B. Adult-onset disease does not fit a 4-month-old infant.

- C. Type 1 is the severe infantile form with onset before 6 months.
- D. Type 3 presents after 18 months and is milder.
- E. Type 4 is the adult-onset form.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Use the age of onset to classify the SMA subtype.

questions.stem: Which inheritance pattern and gene are associated with the common 5q form of spinal muscular atrophy?

options.label: A
options.text: Autosomal recessive SMN1 mutation on chromosome 5

questions.correctAnswerText: Autosomal recessive SMN1 mutation on chromosome 5
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include SMA as an autosomal recessive disorder caused by SMN1 mutations on chromosome 5, leading to reduced survival motor neuron protein.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the inheritance and gene association described for SMA.
- B. Dystrophin deletion causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- C. CTG repeat expansion is associated with myotonic dystrophy type 1.

- D. This is not the usual genetic mechanism described for 5q SMA.
- E. NF1 mutations cause neurofibromatosis type 1.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the SMN gene and chromosome number associated with the common SMA form.

questions.stem: Which examination finding is characteristic of severe infantile spinal muscular atrophy?

options.label: C
options.text: Tongue fasciculations with absent deep tendon reflexes

questions.correctAnswerText: Tongue fasciculations with absent deep tendon reflexes
questions.initialExplanation: Severe SMA type 1 causes lower motor neuron signs, including severe hypotonia, symmetrical weakness, tongue fasciculations, and absent reflexes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Intention tremor and nystagmus suggest cerebellar dysfunction.

- B. Hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses indicate upper motor neuron involvement.
- C. Tongue fasciculations and areflexia are characteristic of SMA type 1.
- D. Calf pseudohypertrophy is associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- E. Fluctuating ptosis with normal reflexes suggests myasthenia gravis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Look for lower motor neuron signs in an infant with profound hypotonia.

questions.stem: Which laboratory finding is expected in classic SMA type 1,?

options.label: E
options.text: Very low serum sodium in each case

questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes a normal creatine kinase level in SMA, helping distinguish it from primary muscle disorders such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. A normal CK is the expected finding listed for SMA.
- B. Bilirubin is not the defining laboratory marker.
- C. Anti-AChR antibodies are associated with autoimmune myasthenia gravis.

- D. Marked CK elevation is characteristic of muscular dystrophy rather than SMA.
- E. Sodium is not the diagnostic marker for SMA.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Differentiate an anterior horn cell disorder from a primary muscle fiber disease.

## Guillain-Barre Syndrome

questions.stem: A child develops progressive symmetrical ascending flaccid weakness 2–3 weeks after gastroenteritis. Deep tendon reflexes are absent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Guillain–Barré syndrome is an acute post-infectious autoimmune polyneuropathy that classically causes symmetrical ascending flaccid paralysis and areflexia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness, typically with ocular or bulbar involvement, and reflexes are usually preserved.

- B. This is the classic presentation of GBS described.
- C. Spastic CP is a chronic non-progressive upper motor neuron disorder.
- D. Juvenile dermatomyositis causes proximal muscle weakness with characteristic skin findings.
- E. Duchenne muscular dystrophy causes progressive proximal weakness over years, not acute ascending paralysis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The preceding infection, ascending pattern, symmetry, and areflexia are key clues.

questions.stem: Which additional feature may occur in Guillain–Barré syndrome due to autonomic nervous system involvement?
questions.initialExplanation: GBS may involve autonomic nerves, causing heart-rate and blood-pressure instability, arrhythmias, urinary retention, ileus, or impaired sweating.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. GBS can cause bilateral facial weakness, but isolated unilateral facial weakness is not the key autonomic feature.

- B. Extensor plantar responses indicate upper motor neuron involvement.
- C. These are autonomic manifestations listed.
- D. Calf pseudohypertrophy is associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- E. Anosmia is not the autonomic manifestation described.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Remember that GBS can affect autonomic as well as motor and sensory nerves.

questions.stem: Which CSF finding is characteristic of Guillain–Barré syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Positive bacterial culture in most cases

options.label: C
options.text: High protein with a normal white-cell count

options.label: E
options.text: High white-cell count with low protein

questions.correctAnswerText: High protein with a normal white-cell count
questions.initialExplanation: Albuminocytologic dissociation—elevated CSF protein with a normal cell count—is characteristic of GBS, often becoming apparent during the second week.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. GBS is an autoimmune neuropathy and CSF culture is not normally positive.
- B. This is not the expected CSF pattern.
- C. This is the characteristic CSF pattern in GBS.
- D. Low glucose with lymphocytes suggests other infectious processes rather than typical GBS.

- E. Marked pleocytosis is not the typical albuminocytologic dissociation pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the term albuminocytologic dissociation and what it means.

questions.stem: Which treatment is identified as the specific treatment of choice for Guillain–Barré syndrome?
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include IV immunoglobulin as the specific treatment of choice; plasma exchange is another specific treatment option.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Corticosteroids alone have no beneficial effect in GBS and may delay recovery.
- B. Dopamine agonists are not a treatment for GBS.
- C. IV immunoglobulin is the specific treatment listed as DOC.
- D. Antibiotics do not treat the autoimmune demyelinating neuropathy.

- E. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Choose the immunomodulatory therapy used to shorten the acute immune-mediated neuropathy.

questions.stem: Which statement about corticosteroids in Guillain–Barré syndrome is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: They are the first-line disease-modifying treatment

options.label: D
options.text: They are required for each mild case

options.label: E
options.text: They have no beneficial effect and may delay recovery

questions.correctAnswerText: They have no beneficial effect and may delay recovery
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance explicitly states that corticosteroids have no beneficial effect in GBS and may delay recovery.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Respiratory monitoring is essential in GBS and cannot be replaced by medication.

- B. IVIG or plasma exchange are the specific treatments listed, not corticosteroid monotherapy.
- C. They do not immediately reverse peripheral nerve demyelination.
- D. Corticosteroids are not recommended as required therapy for every mild case.
- E. This is the statement.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the explicit distinction between IVIG/plasma exchange and corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A patient with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia presents after an infection. Which GBS variant is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Miller Fisher syndrome is a variant of GBS characterized by the triad of external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. West syndrome causes infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia.
- B. Bell palsy causes isolated lower motor neuron facial weakness.
- C. Lennox–Gastaut syndrome is an epilepsy syndrome.
- D. Ataxic CP is a static developmental motor disorder, not an acute post-infectious areflexic syndrome.

- E. This is the classic triad of Miller Fisher syndrome.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the three-part clinical triad associated with this GBS variant.

questions.stem: Which feature helps distinguish Guillain–Barré syndrome from poliomyelitis 's comparison?

options.label: B
options.text: GBS usually causes symmetrical paralysis, whereas poliomyelitis is often asymmetrical

options.label: C
options.text: Poliomyelitis is a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy

options.label: D
options.text: GBS is a pure motor anterior horn cell disorder in typical presentations

options.label: E
options.text: Poliomyelitis causes high CSF protein with normal cells

questions.correctAnswerText: GBS usually causes symmetrical paralysis, whereas poliomyelitis is often asymmetrical

- B. This is the key clinical distinction in the comparison table.
- C. Poliomyelitis affects anterior horn cells rather than causing the peripheral demyelination typical of GBS.

- D. A pure motor anterior horn cell lesion describes poliomyelitis, not GBS.
- E. Polio is associated with CSF pleocytosis rather than the classic albuminocytologic dissociation of GBS.

questions.stem: Which immediate complication must be actively monitored for in a child with Guillain–Barré syndrome?

options.label: D
options.text: Respiratory muscle weakness and respiratory failure

questions.correctAnswerText: Respiratory muscle weakness and respiratory failure
questions.initialExplanation: GBS can involve bulbar and respiratory muscles, causing aspiration, respiratory depression, and respiratory failure; admission and respiratory monitoring are essential.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. CP is a non-progressive developmental motor disorder.
- B. Pyloric obstruction is unrelated to GBS.
- C. Celiac crisis is an intestinal complication of celiac disease.

- D. This is the major acute life-threatening complication described.
- E. Acute glaucoma is not a typical complication.

- Weakness may ascend to involve bulbar and respiratory muscles.

## Duchenne and Becker Muscular Dystrophy

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has frequent falls, difficulty running, a waddling gait, and uses his hands to climb up his thighs when rising from the floor. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy presents in early childhood with progressive proximal weakness, frequent falls, waddling gait, and a positive Gower sign.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Myasthenia causes fatigability, often with ocular or bulbar symptoms.
- B. This is the classic early clinical pattern of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- C. Juvenile dermatomyositis causes proximal weakness with characteristic inflammatory skin findings.

- D. GBS causes acute or subacute ascending weakness and areflexia.
- E. Spastic CP is a non-progressive upper motor neuron disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The age, progressive proximal weakness, and maneuver used to rise from the floor are key clues.

questions.stem: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by deficiency of which protein?
questions.initialExplanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy results from mutations in the dystrophin gene, leading to absent or deficient dystrophin and progressive muscle fiber degeneration.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are associated with autoimmune myasthenia gravis.
- B. Frataxin deficiency causes Friedreich ataxia.
- C. Neurofibromin deficiency causes neurofibromatosis type 1.

- D. SMN protein deficiency is associated with spinal muscular atrophy.
- E. Dystrophin deficiency is the defining molecular defect in DMD.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Recall the structural muscle protein encoded on the X chromosome.

questions.stem: Which inheritance pattern is characteristic of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
questions.initialExplanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder, predominantly affecting boys, with female carriers.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Autosomal recessive inheritance is typical of many other neuromuscular disorders but not DMD.
- B. Autosomal dominant inheritance is not the pattern described for DMD.
- C. Y-linked inheritance is not the mechanism described.

- D. Mitochondrial inheritance is not the pattern for DMD.
- E. This is the inheritance pattern stated.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Consider why boys are predominantly affected while females may be carriers.

questions.stem: Which laboratory finding is expected in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

options.label: B
options.text: Low serum creatine kinase with high CSF protein

questions.initialExplanation: Serum creatine kinase (CK/CPK) is markedly elevated in Duchenne muscular dystrophy because of ongoing skeletal muscle fiber damage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. A normal CK would be inconsistent with typical untreated DMD.
- B. High CSF protein with normal cells is associated with GBS, not DMD.
- C. Low zinc is associated with acrodermatitis enteropathica.

- D. Anti-AChR antibodies support autoimmune myasthenia gravis.
- E. Marked CK elevation is a characteristic investigation finding in DMD.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Think of an enzyme released into blood by damaged muscle fibers.

questions.stem: A boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy develops enlarged-looking calf muscles. What is the mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: Replacement of degenerating muscle by fat and fibrous tissue

options.label: C
options.text: Acute inflammatory edema of the calves

options.label: D
options.text: True increase in contractile muscle mass

options.label: E
options.text: Accumulation of glycogen inside motor neurons

questions.correctAnswerText: Replacement of degenerating muscle by fat and fibrous tissue
questions.initialExplanation: Calf pseudohypertrophy in DMD results from replacement of degenerating muscle fibers by fat and connective tissue rather than true muscle strength or mass.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the mechanism described.
- B. Peripheral nerve hypertrophy does not explain the calf appearance.

- C. Inflammatory edema is not the usual mechanism of calf pseudohypertrophy in DMD.
- D. The enlargement is pseudo-hypertrophy and does not reflect increased functional muscle.
- E. Glycogen accumulation in motor neurons is not the mechanism.
questions.highYieldPoints: - The apparent enlargement does not mean the muscle is stronger.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes Becker muscular dystrophy from Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

options.label: A
options.text: Becker disease is an acute post-infectious neuropathy

options.label: B
options.text: Becker disease is a non-progressive brain injury

options.label: C
options.text: Becker disease is usually milder and progresses more slowly because some functional dystrophin remains

options.label: D
options.text: Becker disease is typically more severe and begins at birth

options.label: E
options.text: Becker disease is caused by antibodies against acetylcholine receptors

questions.correctAnswerText: Becker disease is usually milder and progresses more slowly because some functional dystrophin remains
questions.initialExplanation: Becker muscular dystrophy is similar to DMD but usually has a later onset and milder, slower course because some functional dystrophin is present.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. An acute post-infectious neuropathy describes GBS.
- B. A non-progressive brain injury describes the basis of CP, not Becker muscular dystrophy.

- C. This is the distinction given.
- D. Becker disease is usually milder and later in onset than DMD.
- E. Anti-AChR antibodies are associated with myasthenia gravis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Compare the amount of functional dystrophin and the rate of progression.

questions.stem: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is associated with which genetic mechanism?

options.label: C
options.text: Autosomal dominant CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion

questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include myotonic dystrophy type 1 as an autosomal dominant disorder caused by CTG repeat expansion.

- A. SMN1 mutation causes spinal muscular atrophy.
- B. NF1 mutation causes neurofibromatosis type 1.
- C. This is the genetic mechanism stated for myotonic dystrophy type 1.
- D. This is not the inheritance or repeat mechanism described.

questions.stem: A child has delayed relaxation after firmly gripping an examiner's hand. This phenomenon is called:
questions.initialExplanation: Myotonia is delayed relaxation after muscle contraction, a characteristic feature of myotonic dystrophy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Clonus is rhythmic involuntary contraction following sudden stretch.
- B. Athetosis is slow writhing involuntary movement.
- C. Fasciculations are spontaneous visible muscle fiber twitches associated with denervation.
- D. This is the defining clinical phenomenon described.
- E. Spasticity is velocity-dependent increased tone associated with upper motor neuron lesions.
questions.highYieldPoints:
